claim: Failed T cell-based immunotherapies in the presence of genomic alterations in antigen presentations pathways may be overcome by NK cell-based immunotherapy.
source: Failed T cell-based immunotherapies in the presence of genomic alterations in antigen presentations pathways may be overcome by NK cell-based immunotherapy.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic approaches based on the premise of the study.

claim: NK cell-based immunotherapy may be limited by the presence of immunosuppressive myeloid populations.
source: This approach may still be limited by the presence of immunosuppressive myeloid populations.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific understanding of tumor immunology.

claim: haNKs engineered to express a PD-L1 chimeric antigen receptor killed a panel of human and murine head and neck cancer cells at low effector-to-target ratios in a PD-L1-dependent fashion.
source: Here, we demonstrate that NK cells (haNKs) engineered to express a PD-L1 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) haNKs killed a panel of human and murine head and neck cancer cells at low effector-to-target ratios in a PD-L1-dependent fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1, 2, and 3 showing impedance analysis of tumor cell killing.

claim: Treatment of syngeneic tumors with PD-L1 CAR haNKs resulted in CD8 and PD-L1-dependent tumor rejection or growth inhibition.
source: Treatment of syngeneic tumors resulted in CD8 and PD-L1-dependent tumor rejection or growth inhibition and a reduction in myeloid cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 4, including depletion studies.

claim: Treatment of syngeneic tumors with PD-L1 CAR haNKs resulted in a reduction in myeloid cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1.
source: Treatment of syngeneic tumors resulted in CD8 and PD-L1-dependent tumor rejection or growth inhibition and a reduction in myeloid cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Treatment of xenograft tumors with PD-L1 CAR haNKs resulted in PD-L1-dependent tumor growth inhibition.
source: Treatment of xenograft tumors resulted in PD-L1-dependent tumor growth inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in NSG mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs reduced levels of macrophages and other myeloid cells endogenously expressing high PD-L1 in peripheral blood from patients with head and neck cancer.
source: PD-L1 CAR haNKs reduced levels of macrophages and other myeloid cells endogenously expressing high PD-L1 in peripheral blood from patients with head and neck cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo co-incubation experiments with patient samples shown in Figure 7.

claim: T cell-based immunotherapy is limited by the ability of T cells to detect major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-presented antigen by tumor cells.
source: T cell-based immunotherapy, such as immune checkpoint blockade or adoptive T cell transfer, is limited by the ability of T cells to detect major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-presented antigen by tumor cells.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about T cell recognition mechanisms.

claim: Subpopulations of tumor cells acquire mutations that lead to defective type II interferon (IFN) responses and altered antigen processing and presentation through selective immune pressure during tumorigenesis and progression and genomic instability.
source: Through selective immune pressure during tumorigenesis and progression and genomic instability, subpopulations of tumor cells acquire mutations that lead to defective type II interferon (IFN) responses and altered antigen processing and presentation (Sucker et al., 2014; TRACERx Consortium et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The presence of mutations in antigen processing and presentation pathways predicts failure to respond to immune checkpoint blockade and adoptive T cell transfer immunotherapy.
source: The presence of these mutations predicts failure to respond to immune checkpoint blockade and adoptive T cell transfer immunotherapy (Doran et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2017; Zaretsky et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Natural killer (NK) cell-based immunotherapy may overcome genetic mechanisms of resistance to T cell-based immunotherapy through antigen- and MHC-independent recognition of malignant cells.
source: Natural killer (NK) cell-based immunotherapy may overcome genetic mechanisms of resistance to T cell-based immunotherapy through antigen- and MHC-independent recognition of malignant cells.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge of NK cell biology and represents a logical inference for the therapeutic approach.

claim: NK cells express germ-line receptors that are either stimulatory or inhibitory, and the summation of these signals determines activation status.
source: NK cells express germ-line receptors that are either stimulatory or inhibitory, and the summation of these signals determines activation status (Caligiuri, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: NK-92 cells are derived from a Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patient.
source: NK-92 cells, derived from a Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patient, can be continuously expanded in culture and following irradiation, can be safely administered in high doses to patients with cancer (Gong et al., 1994; Williams et al., 2017; Tonn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original work describing NK-92 cells.

claim: NK-92 cells can be continuously expanded in culture.
source: NK-92 cells, derived from a Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patient, can be continuously expanded in culture and following irradiation, can be safely administered in high doses to patients with cancer (Gong et al., 1994; Williams et al., 2017; Tonn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Following irradiation, NK-92 cells can be safely administered in high doses to patients with cancer.
source: NK-92 cells, derived from a Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patient, can be continuously expanded in culture and following irradiation, can be safely administered in high doses to patients with cancer (Gong et al., 1994; Williams et al., 2017; Tonn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: High-affinity NK (haNK) cells are NK-92 cells engineered to express endoplasmic reticulum-retained IL-2(11).
source: High-affinity NK (haNK) cells are NK-92 cells engineered to express endoplasmic reticulum-retained IL-2(11), have demonstrated potent effector function in numerous pre-clinical models (Friedman et al., 2019; Friedman et al., 2018), and following irradiation, can also be safely administered in high doses to patients (Seery et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the haNK cell product used in the study.

claim: haNKs have demonstrated potent effector function in numerous pre-clinical models.
source: High-affinity NK (haNK) cells are NK-92 cells engineered to express endoplasmic reticulum-retained IL-2(11), have demonstrated potent effector function in numerous pre-clinical models (Friedman et al., 2019; Friedman et al., 2018), and following irradiation, can also be safely administered in high doses to patients (Seery et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Following irradiation, haNKs can be safely administered in high doses to patients.
source: High-affinity NK (haNK) cells are NK-92 cells engineered to express endoplasmic reticulum-retained IL-2(11), have demonstrated potent effector function in numerous pre-clinical models (Friedman et al., 2019; Friedman et al., 2018), and following irradiation, can also be safely administered in high doses to patients (Seery et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: Barriers within the tumor microenvironment such as the presence of immunosuppressive myeloid cells can limit the activation and function of NK cells.
source: However, barriers within the tumor microenvironment that further limit T cell activation and function such as the presence of immunosuppressive myeloid cells also can limit the activation and function of NK cells (Condamine et al., 2016; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Addressing the presence of immunosuppressive myeloid cell populations in the periphery and tumor microenvironment of patients with cancer is likely to be required for effective NK cell-based immunotherapy.
source: Thus, addressing the presence of immunosuppressive myeloid cell populations in the periphery and tumor microenvironment of patients with cancer is likely to be required for effective NK cell-based immunotherapy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known limitations of NK cell therapy.

claim: The PD-L1 CAR includes a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) derived from NANT-601, an IgG1 mAb targeting PD-L1, along with a CD8 hinge, a CD28 transmembrane domain and an intracellular FcεR1γ signaling domain.
source: This second-generation CAR includes a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) derived from NANT-601, and IgG1 mAb targeting PD-L1, along with a CD8 hinge, a CD28 transmembrane domain and an intracellular FcεR1γ signaling domain (diagramed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the CAR construct design, supported by a schematic diagram.

claim: Expression of the PD-L1 CAR was verified on PD-L1 CAR haNK cells by flow cytometry.
source: Expression of the PD-L1 CAR was verified on PD-L1 CAR haNK cells by flow cytometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Exposure to IFNγ significantly increased PD-L1 expression on all human HNSCC cell lines tested.
source: Exposure to IFNγ significantly increased PD-L1 expression on all cells (left panels, Figure 1A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Exposure of cells to IFNγ consistently increased MHC class I expression.
source: Exposure of cells to IFNγ also consistently increased MHC class I expression, but variably decreased expression of NKG2D ligands MHC class I polypeptide-related sequence A/B (MICA/B) on target cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Exposure of cells to IFNγ variably decreased expression of NKG2D ligands MICA/B on target cells.
source: Exposure of cells to IFNγ also consistently increased MHC class I expression, but variably decreased expression of NKG2D ligands MHC class I polypeptide-related sequence A/B (MICA/B) on target cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Killing of HNSCC cells by PD-L1 CAR haNKs at low effector-to-target ratios (0.5:1 or 1:1) was significantly greater compared to haNKs in the absence of IFNγ pre-treatment of target cells.
source: As measured by real-time impedance analysis (middle and right panels, Figure 1A–E), killing of HNSCC cells by PD-L1 CAR haNKs at low effector-to-target ratios (0.5:1 or 1:1) was significantly greater compared to haNKs in the absence of IFNγ pre-treatment of target cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Pre-treatment of target cells with IFNγ significantly increased killing by PD-L1 CAR haNKs but did not increase killing by haNKs.
source: Pre-treatment of target cells with IFNγ significantly increased killing by PD-L1 CAR haNKs but did not increase killing by haNKs.
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Killing of IFNγ pre-treated human target cells by PD-L1 CAR haNKs was durable as no tumor cell growth rebound was observed.
source: Killing of IFNγ pre-treated human target cells by PD-L1 CAR haNKs was durable as no tumor cell growth rebound was observed.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of impedance curves over time in Figure 1.

claim: No clear correlation between HLA class I or MICA/B expression and killing by PD-L1 CAR haNKs or haNKs existed.
source: No clear correlation between HLA class I or MICA/B expression and killing by PD-L1 CAR haNKs or haNKs existed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 with killing data in Figure 1.

claim: At matched effector-to-target ratios, PD-L1 CAR haNKs kill multiple human HNSCC targets to a greater degree than haNKs.
source: These data suggested that at matched effector-to-target ratios, PD-L1 CAR haNKs kill multiple human HNSCC targets to a greater degree than haNKs, and that susceptibility to PD-L1 CAR haNK killing can be increased with greater PD-L1 expression following IFNγ pre-treatment of target cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the impedance analysis data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Susceptibility to PD-L1 CAR haNK killing can be increased with greater PD-L1 expression following IFNγ pre-treatment of target cells.
source: These data suggested that at matched effector-to-target ratios, PD-L1 CAR haNKs kill multiple human HNSCC targets to a greater degree than haNKs, and that susceptibility to PD-L1 CAR haNK killing can be increased with greater PD-L1 expression following IFNγ pre-treatment of target cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between IFNγ-induced PD-L1 expression and increased killing shown in Figure 1.

claim: Following efficient killing of target cells for a period of 4 hr, PD-L1 CAR haNKs retained their ability to kill target cells albeit at a reduced capacity compared to target-naïve PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
source: Following efficient killing of target cells for a period of 4 hr, PD-L1 CAR haNKs retained their ability to kill target cells albeit at a reduced capacity compared to target-naïve PD-L1 CAR haNKs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Prior exposure to target cells partially reduces but does not abrogate the effector capacity of PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
source: Prior exposure to target cells partially reduces but does not abrogate the effector capacity of PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs killed IFNγ pre-treated murine HNSCC cells in a dose-dependent fashion, with 70–80% cell killing at a 1:1 effector-to-target ratio.
source: PD-L1 CAR haNKs killed IFNγ pre-treated murine HNSCC cells in a dose-dependent fashion, with 70–80% cell killing at a 1:1 effector-to-target ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: In the absence of IFNγ pre-treatment, baseline expression of PD-L1 on murine HNSCC cells was low.
source: In the absence of IFNγ pre-treatment, baseline expression of PD-L1 on murine HNSCC cells was low, and PD-L1 CAR haNks and haNKs killed targets to a similar degree at 1:1 effector-to-target ratios (Figure 2A&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs and haNKs killed murine HNSCC targets to a similar degree at 1:1 effector-to-target ratios in the absence of IFNγ pre-treatment.
source: In the absence of IFNγ pre-treatment, baseline expression of PD-L1 on murine HNSCC cells was low, and PD-L1 CAR haNks and haNKs killed targets to a similar degree at 1:1 effector-to-target ratios (Figure 2A&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: IFNγ pre-treatment significantly increased expression of PD-L1 and killing by PD-L1 CAR haNKs of murine HNSCC cells, but no increase in killing by haNKs was observed.
source: IFNγ pre-treatment significantly increased expression of PD-L1 and killing by PD-L1 CAR haNKs, but no increase in killing by haNKs was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and impedance analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNK killing of IFNγ pre-treated murine target cells was less durable compared to human target cells, with a degree of rebound of target cell growth by 72 hr.
source: PD-L1 CAR haNK killing of IFN pre-treated murine target cells was less durable compared to human target cells, with a degree of rebound of target cell growth by 72 hr.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of impedance curves over time in Figure 2.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs kill murine HNSCC cells to a greater degree than haNKs.
source: These data revealed that PD-L1 CAR haNKs also kill murine HNSCC cells to a greater degree than haNKs, and that PD-L1 CAR haNK killing can be increased with IFNγ-induced PD-L1 expression.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the impedance analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNK killing of murine HNSCC cells can be increased with IFNγ-induced PD-L1 expression.
source: These data revealed that PD-L1 CAR haNKs also kill murine HNSCC cells to a greater degree than haNKs, and that PD-L1 CAR haNK killing can be increased with IFNγ-induced PD-L1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between IFNγ-induced PD-L1 expression and increased killing shown in Figure 2.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing was used to generate PD-L1 knockout cell variants of human UMSCC-1, human UMSCC-11A and murine MOC1 cells.
source: To determine the relative contribution of direct and PD-L1 CAR-mediated killing of human and murine HNSCC targets by PD-L1 CAR haNKs, CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing was used to generate PD-L1 knockout cell variants of human UMSCC-1, human UMSCC-11A and murine MOC1 cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: Exposure of PD-L1 knockout cells to IFNγ demonstrated a lack of baseline and IFNγ-inducible PD-L1 expression but retained baseline and IFNγ-inducible HLA class I expression.
source: Exposure of these PD-L1 knockout cells to IFNγ demonstrated a lack of baseline and IFNγ-inducible PD-L1 expression (compared to isotype control staining) but retained baseline and IFNγ-inducible HLA class I expression, demonstrating that overall IFNγ responses remained intact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Killing of IFNγ pre-treated parental cells by PD-L1 CAR haNKs was nearly complete.
source: Although killing of IFNγ pre-treated parental cells was nearly complete, killing of PD-L1 knockout cells ranged from 10–40%, suggesting that 10–40% of PD-L1 CAR haNK killing is due to direct NK cytotoxicity and independent of the PD-L1 CAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Killing of PD-L1 knockout cells by PD-L1 CAR haNKs ranged from 10–40%.
source: Although killing of IFNγ pre-treated parental cells was nearly complete, killing of PD-L1 knockout cells ranged from 10–40%, suggesting that 10–40% of PD-L1 CAR haNK killing is due to direct NK cytotoxicity and independent of the PD-L1 CAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 10–40% of PD-L1 CAR haNK killing is due to direct NK cytotoxicity and independent of the PD-L1 CAR.
source: Although killing of IFNγ pre-treated parental cells was nearly complete, killing of PD-L1 knockout cells ranged from 10–40%, suggesting that 10–40% of PD-L1 CAR haNK killing is due to direct NK cytotoxicity and independent of the PD-L1 CAR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential killing of parental vs. PD-L1 knockout cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: Increased PD-L1 CAR haNK killing of targets correlated with increased ratios of parental-to-PD-L1 knockout cells.
source: Increased PD-L1 CAR haNK killing of targets correlated with increased ratios of parental-to-PD-L1 knockout cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by impedance analysis data of mixed cell populations shown in Figure 3.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs utilize both direct and PD-L1 CAR-dependent killing of human and murine HNSCC cells.
source: These data demonstrated that PD-L1 CAR haNKs utilize both direct and PD-L1 CAR-dependent killing of human and murine HNSCC cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNK monotherapy induced tumor rejection in 30% of treated mice bearing MOC1 tumors.
source: PD-L1 CAR haNK monotherapy induced tumor rejection in 30% of treated mice and tumor growth inhibition in a subset of remaining mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNK monotherapy induced tumor growth inhibition in a subset of mice bearing MOC1 tumors that did not reject tumors.
source: PD-L1 CAR haNK monotherapy induced tumor rejection in 30% of treated mice and tumor growth inhibition in a subset of remaining mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No weight loss, alterations in select blood chemistries, or other measurable forms of toxicity were observed with systemic PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment administered via intravenous or intraperitoneal routes.
source: No weight loss, alterations in select blood chemistries, or other measurable forms of toxicity were observed with systemic PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment administered via intravenous or intraperitoneal routes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight and blood chemistry data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Tumor rejection by PD-L1 CAR haNKs was abrogated in mice bearing PD-L1 knockout MOC1 tumors.
source: Tumor rejection was abrogated in mice bearing PD-L1 knockout MOC1 tumors (Figure 4B), but heterogeneous tumor growth inhibition was still observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Heterogeneous tumor growth inhibition was still observed in mice bearing PD-L1 knockout MOC1 tumors treated with PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
source: Tumor rejection was abrogated in mice bearing PD-L1 knockout MOC1 tumors (Figure 4B), but heterogeneous tumor growth inhibition was still observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IFNγ is a primary driver of PD-L1 expression on MOC1 tumor cells.
source: IFNγ is a primary driver of PD-L1 expression on MOC1 tumor cells (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior published work.

claim: IFNγ or CD8 depletion abrogated the anti-tumor effect of PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
source: IFNγ or CD8 depletion abrogated the anti-tumor effect of PD-L1 CAR haNKs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data with antibody depletions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Depletion of TNFα did not alter the anti-tumor effect of PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
source: Depletion of TNFα did not alter the anti-tumor effect of PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data with antibody depletions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IFNγ produced by CD8 T cells is the major driver of tumor cell PD-L1 expression being targeted by PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
source: This data suggested that IFNγ produced by CD8 T cells was the major driver of tumor cell PD-L1 expression being targeted by PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the depletion studies shown in Figure 4C and PD-L1 expression data in Figure 4D.

claim: Tumor cell-specific PD-L1 expression was significantly increased after PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment.
source: Tumor cell-specific PD-L1 expression was significantly increased after PD-L1 CAR haNKs, and this increase was abrogated in the presence of CD8 depletion (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in tumor cell-specific PD-L1 expression after PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment was abrogated in the presence of CD8 depletion.
source: Tumor cell-specific PD-L1 expression was significantly increased after PD-L1 CAR haNKs, and this increase was abrogated in the presence of CD8 depletion (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs can induce PD-L1-dependent tumor rejection in a syngeneic murine system.
source: These data suggested that PD-L1 CAR haNKs can induce PD-L1-dependent tumor rejection in a syngeneic murine system, and that CD8 T cells are a primary source of IFNγ driving tumor cell PD-L1 expression in this model.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the in vivo data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CD8 T cells are a primary source of IFNγ driving tumor cell PD-L1 expression in the MOC1 tumor model.
source: These data suggested that PD-L1 CAR haNKs can induce PD-L1-dependent tumor rejection in a syngeneic murine system, and that CD8 T cells are a primary source of IFNγ driving tumor cell PD-L1 expression in this model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the depletion studies shown in Figure 4C and PD-L1 expression data in Figure 4D.

claim: In the periphery of tumor bearing mice, PD-L1 was uniformly expressed on macrophages and Ly6Ghi neutrophilic myeloid cells to a greater degree compared to other cell types.
source: In the periphery of tumor bearing mice, PD-L1 was uniformly expressed on macrophages and Ly6Ghi neutrophilic myeloid cells to a greater degree compared to other cells types.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Macrophages and neutrophilic myeloid cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1 were decreased in the spleen compared to control following PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment.
source: Quantification of splenic immune cell fractions revealed that macrophages and neutrophilic myeloid cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1 were decreased compared to control following treatment, whereas no changes were observed in other immune subsets (Figure 5B&C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: No changes were observed in other splenic immune subsets following PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment.
source: Quantification of splenic immune cell fractions revealed that macrophages and neutrophilic myeloid cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1 were decreased compared to control following treatment, whereas no changes were observed in other immune subsets (Figure 5B&C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: In the tumor microenvironment, PD-L1 was expressed to a greater degree on macrophages, neutrophilic and monocytic myeloid cells compared to tumor cells or other immune subsets.
source: In the tumor microenvironment, PD-L1 was expressed to a greater degree on macrophages, neutrophilic and monocytic myeloid cells compared to tumor cells or other immune subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis 1 hr after treatment verified the presence of adoptively transferred PD-L1 CAR haNKs in the blood, spleens and tumors of MOC1 tumor bearing mice.
source: Flow cytometric analysis 1 hr after treatment verified the presence of adoptively transferred PD-L1 CAR haNKs in the blood, spleens and tumors of MOC1 tumor bearing mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Quantification of tumor immune infiltration revealed decreased macrophages, neutrophilic and monocytic myeloid cells following PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment.
source: Quantification of tumor immune infiltration revealed decreased macrophages, neutrophilic and monocytic myeloid cells, increased CD8 and CD4 T-lymphocytes, and no change in Tregs or NK cells following treatment (Figure 5B&D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: Quantification of tumor immune infiltration revealed increased CD8 and CD4 T-lymphocytes following PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment.
source: Quantification of tumor immune infiltration revealed decreased macrophages, neutrophilic and monocytic myeloid cells, increased CD8 and CD4 T-lymphocytes, and no change in Tregs or NK cells following treatment (Figure 5B&D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: Quantification of tumor immune infiltration revealed no change in Tregs or NK cells following PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment.
source: Quantification of tumor immune infiltration revealed decreased macrophages, neutrophilic and monocytic myeloid cells, increased CD8 and CD4 T-lymphocytes, and no change in Tregs or NK cells following treatment (Figure 5B&D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: Immune cell subsets from the periphery and tumor that expressed comparatively greater levels of PD-L1 were reduced following 24 hr of co-incubation with PD-L1 CAR haNKs ex vivo.
source: Similar to results observed in vivo, immune cell subsets from the periphery and tumor that expressed comparatively greater levels of PD-L1 were reduced following 24 hr of co-incubation with PD-L1 CAR haNKs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo co-incubation data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs can mediate reduction of immune cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1 in the periphery and tumor microenvironment of MOC1 tumor-bearing wild-type mice.
source: Cumulatively, these data exhibited that PD-L1 CAR haNKs can mediate reduction of immune cells endogenously expressing high levels of PD-L1 in the periphery and tumor microenvironment of MOC1 tumor-bearing wild-type mice.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tumor growth inhibition was observed in NSG mice bearing UMSCC-1 human tumors treated with PD-L1 CAR haNKs, but no tumors were rejected.
source: Tumor growth inhibition was observed, but no tumors were rejected (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tumor growth inhibition following PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment was abrogated in NSG mice bearing PD-L1 knockout UMSCC-1 tumors.
source: Tumor growth inhibition following PD-L1 CAR haNK treatment was abrogated in NSG mice bearing PD-L1 knockout UMSCC-1 tumors (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tumor cell-specific PD-L1 expression within UMSCC-1 tumors was increased following treatment with PD-L1 CAR haNKs.
source: Flow cytometry and immunofluorescence were used to verify that tumor cell-specific PD-L1 expression within UMSCC-1 tumors was increased following treatment with PD-L1 CAR haNKs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs produce IFNγ at rest.
source: PD-L1 CAR haNKs produce IFNγ at rest, and to a higher degree following target engagement (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs produce IFNγ to a higher degree following target engagement.
source: PD-L1 CAR haNKs produce IFNγ at rest, and to a higher degree following target engagement (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs may be the source of the IFNγ leading to increased expression of PD-L1 on the UMSCC-1 tumor cells.
source: These data suggested that the PD-L1 CAR haNKs may be the source of the IFNγ leading to increased expression of PD-L1 on the UMSCC-1 tumor cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IFNγ production data and PD-L1 expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs can mediate PD-L1-dependent tumor growth inhibition in immunodeficient mice bearing human HNSCCs.
source: Cumulatively, these data demonstrated that PD-L1 CAR haNKs can also mediate PD-L1-dependent tumor growth inhibition in immunodeficient mice bearing human HNSCCs, possibly through the ability of PD-L1 CAR haNKs to induce IFNγ-dependent PD-L1 expression on tumor cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the in vivo data shown in Figure 6.

claim: PD-L1 CAR haNKs can mediate PD-L1-dependent tumor growth inhibition in immunodeficient mice possibly through the ability of PD-L1 CAR haNKs to induce IFNγ-dependent PD-L1 expression on tumor cells.
source: Cumulatively, these data demonstrated that PD-L1 CAR haNKs can also mediate PD-L1-dependent tumor growth inhibition in immunodeficient mice bearing human HNSCCs, possibly through the ability of PD-L1 CAR haNKs to induce IFNγ-dependent PD-L1 expression on tumor cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the peripheral blood of HNSCC patients, macrophages expressed the greatest levels of PD-L1.
source: In the peripheral blood of HNSCC patients, macrophages expressed the greatest levels of PD-L1, and CD14+ and CD15+ myeloid subsets expressed greater levels of PD-L1 compared to lymphoid or NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data from patient samples shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Killing of targets by PD-L1 CAR haNKs was primarily PD-L1-dependent as tumor cell PD-L1 knockout reduced in vitro killing capacity by 60–90% and abrogated in vivo tumor rejection or growth inhibition.
source: Although PD-L1 CAR haNKs mediated cytotoxicity through both direct and PD-L1 CAR-dependent mechanisms, killing of targets was primary PD-L1-dependent as tumor cell PD-L1 knockout reduced in vitro killing capacity by 60–90% and abrogated in vivo tumor rejection or growth inhibition.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 6.
